label: Mishlei (Proverbs) — Part 2 — Chapters 11–20
summary_plain: Mishlei chapters 11 through 20 deliver the core proverbial wisdom of Shelomoh. These are paired contrasts: the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the fool, the diligent and the lazy. A false balance is an abomination to YHWH, but a just weight is his delight. The tongue of the righteous is choice silver. Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge. The name of YHWH is a strong tower — the righteous run into it and are safe. A friend loves at all times. Even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads Mishlei 11-20 from DSS Proverbs fragments (4QProv-a, 4QProv-b) and the Orit Ge'ez. These chapters form the dense core of Shelomoh's mashal collection — antithetical parallelism in its purest form. The instruction on honest weights and measures (11:1, 16:11, 20:10, 20:23) connects to the Egyptian Ma'at tradition — justice, balance, and cosmic order as the foundation of wisdom. The Instructions of Amenemope contain the same emphasis on honest scales. The Hebrew wisdom tradition and the Egyptian wisdom tradition are sister branches of the same Afro-Asiatic intellectual heritage. The proverbs on speech — the tongue, the lips, the mouth — form the largest thematic cluster, reflecting the Afro-Asiatic understanding that language creates and destroys reality.

key_terms.definition: Mishlei 16:18: 'Pride goes before destruction and a haughty spirit before a fall' — one of the most foundational wisdom warnings in the Hebrew tradition.
Mishlei 22:1: 'A good name is more desirable than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold' — a core value statement about reputation and character.
Mishlei 22:6: 'Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it' — the foundational covenant-education principle.
The collection in Mishlei 30:1-33, attributed to Agur son of Yaqeh; contains the question 'Who has ascended to heaven and come down?' (30:4) — an ancient text the NT later borrowed from.

Mishlei 30:4: 'Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? What is his name, and what is his son's name?' — ancient source; the NT borrowed from Agur's rhetorical question.
The acrostic poem closing Mishlei (31:10-31), describing a capable, wise, industrious woman; she fears YHWH and is praised at the city gates — the structural bookend to Lady Wisdom in chs 1-9.
Mishlei 31:1-9, attributed to King Lemuel — 'the words that his mother taught him'; warns against women who destroy kings, drunkenness, and urges defense of the poor and needy.
The 'three things / four things' pattern in Mishlei (chs 30, 6:16) and other wisdom texts; a literary device for cataloguing related phenomena for reflection.
The structural contrast running through Mishlei: Wisdom (chs 1-9, 31) invites to life; Folly (9:13-18) steals and leads to Sheol — representing every choice between YHWH's path and destruction.

Mishlei is not a continuous composition but an anthology of distinct collections: chs 1-9 (instruction essays), 10-22:16 (Shlomo sayings), 22:17-24:22 (Words of the Wise), 25-29 (Khizkiyahu's collection), 30 (Agur), 31 (Lemuel + Eshet Khayil).

faq.question: What is the Eshet Khayil and why does it close the book of Mishlei?
faq.answer: The Eshet Khayil (Woman of Valor, Mishlei 31:10-31) is an aleph-bet acrostic poem praising a capable, industrious, wise woman who fears YHWH. It closes Mishlei deliberately as a bookend to Lady Wisdom in chs 1-9: the whole book opens with personified Wisdom calling in the streets and closes with a flesh-and-blood embodiment of that wisdom, praised at the city gates.

faq.question: What is the significance of Agur's question in Mishlei 30:4?
faq.answer: Agur asks: 'Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? What is his name, and what is his son's name?' This rhetorical question in the ancient text emphasizes YHWH's incomparability and human limitation. The NT later borrowed this rhetorical form; the direction runs from Mishlei's ancient text to NT adaptation, not the reverse.

faq.question: What is the anthology structure of Mishlei and what does it reveal?
faq.answer: Mishlei is not a single composition but an anthology: chs 1-9 (extended instruction essays), 10:1-22:16 (Shlomo's proverbs), 22:17-24:22 (Words of the Wise), 25-29 (Khizkiyahu's copied collection), 30 (Words of Agur), 31 (Words of Lemuel + Eshet Khayil). This shows Hebrew wisdom was an ongoing tradition, gathered and preserved across generations and royal courts.

faq.question: How does Mishlei 22:17-24:22 (Words of the Wise) relate to Egyptian wisdom?
faq.answer: This section shows close parallels to the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, demonstrating that Hebrew wisdom engaged with and adapted broader ancient Near Eastern wisdom while reshaping it within the YHWH-covenant framework. This shows ancient Hebrew wisdom was not isolated — it actively engaged with its world while maintaining YHWH as the ultimate foundation.

faq.question: What does Mishlei 29:18 teach about the relationship between prophecy and Torah?
faq.answer: Mishlei 29:18 states: 'Where there is no prophetic vision the people perish; but blessed is he who keeps the Torah.' This pairs the prophetic voice with Torah-keeping as the two guardrails of community life. The absence of either leaves a people without guidance and without structure — both are needed for the covenant community to thrive.

faq.question: What does the numerical saying pattern (three things, four things) in Mishlei 30 teach?
faq.answer: The numerical sayings (30:15-33) catalog related phenomena — things that are never satisfied, things too wonderful to understand, things the earth cannot bear, things that are small but wise. The pattern invites reflection on categories of experience and divine order. By listing and comparing, the reader is trained to observe creation carefully — a core wisdom discipline.

faq.question: What is the relationship between Mishlei's Lemuel section and women's wisdom?
faq.answer: Mishlei 31:1 explicitly states these are 'words that his mother taught him' — a woman's wisdom handed down to a king. This, combined with the Eshet Khayil and Lady Wisdom, makes Mishlei unusual in placing women's wisdom at the beginning, middle, and end of the book. YHWH's wisdom is not exclusively transmitted through male lineage.

faq.question: How does Mishlei 25-29 (Khizkiyahu's collection) differ from the earlier Shlomo sections?
faq.answer: Mishlei 25:1 says these are Shlomo's proverbs copied by Khizkiyahu's scribes — showing that the king who reformed Yehudah's worship (and who encountered the Assyrian crisis of Yesha'yahu's time) also valued preserving wisdom literature. The sayings in this section tend toward more extended comparison proverbs (like simile chains) rather than the simple antithetical parallels of chs 10-15.

faq.question: What does Mishlei say about the connection between laziness and poverty?
faq.answer: Mishlei repeatedly connects sloth and poverty: 10:4 'A slack hand causes poverty, but the hand of the diligent makes rich.' 13:4 'The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied.' 24:33-34 'A little sleep, a little slumber... and poverty will come upon you like a robber.' This is practical covenant living — creation rewards diligence.

faq.question: What does Mishlei 16:1-9 teach about human planning and YHWH's sovereignty?
faq.answer: Mishlei 16 holds two things in tension: humans plan, but YHWH determines the outcome. 16:1: 'The plans of the heart belong to humanity, but the answer of the tongue is from YHWH.' 16:9: 'The heart of a person plans his way, but YHWH establishes his steps.' 16:3: 'Commit your work to YHWH, and your plans will be established.' This is not fatalism but covenant trust — align with YHWH's purposes, and your work is grounded.
